reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Proximal (long head) ruptures are far more common, usually in older patients with pre-existing tendinopathy, and produce a distal 'Popeye' muscle bulge
Distal biceps ruptures typically occur in middle-aged men from a sudden eccentric load to a flexed elbow and cause a proximal retracted bulge
Proximal ruptures cause little functional loss and are usually managed non-operatively
Distal ruptures cause notable loss of supination and flexion strength and are often repaired, especially in active patients
The hook test (inability to hook a finger under the distal biceps tendon) suggests complete distal rupture
Distal rupture is frequently associated with a sudden pop and antecubital pain, bruising and a palpable defect
Anabolic steroid use, smoking and fluoroquinolone exposure are recognised risk factors
reference.pathophysiology: Rupture occurs when tensile load exceeds tendon strength, usually at a site of pre-existing degenerative tendinopathy. Proximal long-head ruptures commonly occur within the bicipital groove or at the labral origin, whereas distal ruptures avulse from the radial tuberosity. Loss of the distal insertion markedly reduces supination power because the biceps is the principal forearm supinator, whereas the long head contributes relatively little to overall elbow function.
additionalDifferentials: Biceps tendinopathy or subluxation without rupture
additionalInvestigations: Clinical hook test and strength assessment for distal ruptures
Ultrasound to confirm and localise the rupture
MRI (flexed-abducted-supinated view) for distal tendon evaluation
redFlags: Complete distal rupture in an active patient where delayed repair becomes difficult
Rapidly enlarging haematoma or neurovascular symptoms in the antecubital fossa
Suspicion of underlying tendon-weakening drug therapy
reference.prognosis: Proximal ruptures leave a cosmetic deformity with minimal strength loss and good functional outcome; distal repairs restore supination and flexion strength well when performed early, whereas chronic retracted tears are more challenging.
pitfalls: Delaying diagnosis of a distal rupture so that primary repair is no longer feasible
Recommending surgery for proximal ruptures whose functional deficit is minimal
Missing radial or posterior interosseous nerve injury during distal repair planning
Confusing a partial tear with a complete rupture without imaging
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Proximal long-head ruptures are managed non-operatively with analgesia, relative rest and progressive physiotherapy, accepting the cosmetic Popeye deformity
Distal biceps rupture is treated with early surgical reattachment to the radial tuberosity, especially in active patients, to restore supination and flexion strength
Analgesia with simple analgesics or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs alongside early graded rehabilitation
Prompt hook-test and imaging assessment with timely surgical referral, since chronic retracted distal tears are far harder to repair
Structured postoperative rehabilitation with staged range-of-movement and strengthening protocols
Orthopaedic or sports-medicine referral to guide the operative-versus-conservative decision according to functional demand
